questions.question: CTA shows an entry tear distal to the left subclavian artery, with retrograde extension into the ascending aorta. Which classification and initial definitive pathway are appropriate?
options: Stanford B; urgent descending-aortic TEVAR
Stanford B; anti-impulse therapy and surveillance
Stanford A; emergency open aortic repair
Stanford A; planned elective repair after stabilization
questions.explanation:
Anatomical Classification of Aortic Dissection

Correct answer: Stanford A; emergency open aortic repair

Classify the Extent

**Stanford depends on ascending involvement, not the entry-tear site.**

Any ascending involvement is A; B spares the ascending aorta. Isolated arch disease may require more detailed contemporary classification.

Clinical Consequence

**Urgent surgical assessment and anti-impulse treatment proceed together.**

Medical stabilization is a bridge to repair, not a reason to defer an operable acute type A lesion.

**DeBakey describes origin and propagation.**

I originates in the ascending aorta and extends beyond it; II is confined to ascending; III originates in descending.

DeBakey III subtype | Extent

IIIa | Descending thoracic, above diaphragm

IIIb | Extends below diaphragm

Stanford B; urgent descending-aortic TEVAR: TEVAR is commonly used for complicated descending dissection; an entry tear there does not negate ascending involvement.

Stanford B; anti-impulse therapy and surveillance: This fits disease sparing the ascending aorta without complications; retrograde ascending involvement changes the Stanford category.

Stanford A; planned elective repair after stabilization: Elective repair suits selected stable chronic disease; acute ascending dissection carries immediate rupture, regurgitation and tamponade risks.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: In type B dissection, renal hypoperfusion varies with pressure. CTA shows compression of the aortic true lumen across the renal ostium without a flap extending into the renal artery. What mechanism predominates?
options: Dynamic branch-vessel obstruction
Static branch-vessel obstruction
Renal artery thromboembolism
Atheroembolic renal disease
questions.explanation:
Dynamic and Static Malperfusion

Correct answer: Dynamic branch-vessel obstruction

Mechanism

**Dynamic:** false-lumen pressure compresses the true lumen and obstructs a branch origin.

Severity can change with the pressure relationship between lumina.

**Static:** the dissection propagates into the branch, producing fixed narrowing or thrombosis.

Treatment Implications

**Malperfusion makes type B dissection complicated.**

Urgent aortic-team treatment is needed; proximal tear coverage may restore true-lumen flow.

**Persistent branch obstruction may need fenestration or branch stenting.**

Monitor lactate, urine output, abdominal findings and limb perfusion; imaging anatomy alone does not quantify organ injury.

Static branch-vessel obstruction: Static obstruction results from dissection entering the branch with fixed stenosis or thrombosis; that branch extension is absent here.

Renal artery thromboembolism: An embolus creates a branch filling defect and generally fixed occlusion; ostial obstruction varying with true-lumen compression suggests a flap mechanism.

Atheroembolic renal disease: Cholesterol emboli affect small vessels, often with skin signs after instrumentation; this is major-ostial perfusion compromise.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: A patient with Marfan syndrome has abrupt, severe tearing chest pain, equal pulses and normal blood pressure, with no new murmur or neurological deficit. What is the ADD-RS?
questions.explanation:
Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score

Correct answer: 2

Scoring

**Count positive categories, not individual features.**

Marfan syndrome gives 1 for predisposition; abrupt/severe/tearing pain collectively gives 1; examination gives 0.

Use in Diagnosis

**A high-risk presentation requires definitive imaging.**

D-dimer is an adjunct in selected low-probability pathways, not a replacement for CTA in this case.

**A normal ECG or chest radiograph does not exclude dissection.**

Intramural hematoma, limited disease or thrombosed false lumen can complicate biomarker interpretation.

Category | Examples; maximum 1 point each

Predisposition | Heritable aortopathy, family history, known aneurysm, recent aortic manipulation

Pain | Abrupt onset, severe intensity, ripping/tearing quality

Examination | Pulse/BP differential, painful neurological deficit or new AR, shock

1: One point would apply if only one risk category were present; this patient has both a predisposing condition and high-risk pain.

3: Three requires a high-risk examination category as well; the supplied examination does not provide one.

4: ADD-RS is capped at three categories; multiple pain descriptors do not each contribute a separate point.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: A hemodynamically stable patient has abrupt severe chest pain maximal at onset, an interarm pulse difference and a new diastolic murmur. ECG shows ischemic changes. Which investigation should be prioritized before committing to an antithrombotic or fibrinolytic ACS pathway?
options: Immediate coronary-only angiography without assessing the aorta
Serial troponin testing as the principal discriminator
D-dimer as a stand-alone exclusion test
Urgent CT angiography directed at suspected acute aortic syndrome
questions.explanation:
Acute Aortic Syndrome Can Present With Myocardial Ischemia

Correct answer: Urgent CT angiography directed at suspected acute aortic syndrome

Recognize the Competing Emergency

**Acute aortic disease can cause coronary malperfusion and ischemic ECG changes.** Those findings do not establish primary coronary atherothrombosis as the cause.

Abrupt maximal pain, pulse or pressure differences and a new aortic regurgitation murmur raise concern in the stated presentation.

A normal chest radiograph would not adequately exclude the diagnosis.

Match Imaging to Stability and Availability

**CT is recommended as initial diagnostic imaging for suspected acute aortic syndrome in suitable patients.** TEE or MRI can be alternatives according to circumstances.

If instability makes transport unsafe, bedside assessment and specialist coordination may favor another rapid imaging route. Begin appropriate monitoring and urgent aortic-team involvement.

Fibrinolysis or indiscriminate anticoagulation can be dangerous when dissection is the actual mechanism, so resolve this specific high-risk differential promptly rather than waiting for a complete biomarker series. This is not a reason to delay reperfusion in every typical coronary presentation; the stem supplies substantial aortic red flags. Document the reasoning and proceed rapidly with definitive care once the anatomy is known. The purpose of recognizing the mimic is to choose the correct emergency pathway, not simply add another diagnosis to a list.

Immediate coronary-only angiography without assessing the aorta: Coronary assessment may become necessary, but the abrupt pain, pulse discrepancy and new regurgitant murmur require urgent evaluation of the suspected aortic emergency.

Serial troponin testing as the principal discriminator: Troponin can identify myocardial injury but cannot exclude aortic dissection or establish whether coronary ischemia is due to aortic involvement.

D-dimer as a stand-alone exclusion test: A low D-dimer can contribute in selected low-probability pathways, but this high-risk presentation requires definitive imaging rather than biomarker exclusion alone.

questions.question: A patient with suspected proximal dissection has shock and cannot safely leave the resuscitation area. An experienced echocardiographer is immediately available. Which test best provides rapid definitive proximal-aortic information?
options: Transthoracic echocardiography alone
Contrast-enhanced whole-aorta CT
Aortic magnetic resonance angiography
Bedside transesophageal echocardiography
questions.explanation:
Imaging an Unstable Suspected Aortic Dissection

Correct answer: Bedside transesophageal echocardiography

Immediate Information

**TEE assesses proximal flap, AR, tamponade and ventricular function.**

It can be performed bedside or in theatre while surgical management is organized.

Limitations and Complementary Imaging

**A negative study is not universally definitive.**

Distal ascending/arch blind regions and operator dependence matter; persistent suspicion requires further assessment.

**CTA maps the entire aorta and branches when feasible.**

ECG gating reduces proximal motion artifact; MRI is useful for selected stable patients and follow-up.

**Avoid delaying emergency repair** merely to obtain every imaging modality when diagnosis and operative need are established.

Transthoracic echocardiography alone: TTE quickly assesses effusion and regurgitation but incompletely visualizes the thoracic aorta; a negative result cannot exclude dissection.

Contrast-enhanced whole-aorta CT: CTA is preferred in most stable patients and maps branch anatomy; unsafe transfer makes bedside TEE the immediate choice.

Aortic magnetic resonance angiography: MRI offers comprehensive imaging without ionizing radiation but is impractical for an unstable patient requiring active resuscitation.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: A hypertensive patient with uncomplicated acute type B dissection has HR 112/min and BP 186/104 mmHg, with preserved perfusion and no beta-blocker contraindication. What is the best initial pharmacological sequence?
options: Oral labetalol followed by oral amlodipine
IV nicardipine, then add esmolol after pressure normalizes
IV nitroprusside followed by oral metoprolol
IV esmolol, then add nicardipine if pressure remains high
questions.explanation:
Anti-Impulse Therapy in Acute Aortic Syndrome

Correct answer: IV esmolol, then add nicardipine if pressure remains high

Treatment Sequence

**Analgesia and arterial-line monitoring; initiate IV beta-blockade.**

Esmolol: 500 micrograms/kg over 1 minute, then 50 micrograms/kg/min; titrate to response, commonly up to 200 micrograms/kg/min.

**Add IV vasodilator if needed after rate control.**

Nicardipine ==5 mg/hour==; increase ==2.5 mg/hour== every 5–15 minutes, maximum ==15 mg/hour==.

Targets and Safety

**2022 ACC/AHA:** HR 60–80/min; SBP ==<120 mmHg== or the lowest pressure maintaining organ perfusion.

**Monitor bradycardia, AV block, bronchospasm and hypoperfusion.**

Shock, major malperfusion or acute severe AR requires individualized hemodynamic management rather than automatic target chasing.

Control pain and impulse → Reassess perfusion → Add vasodilator if required

Oral labetalol followed by oral amlodipine: Oral drugs suit longer-term control; the acute hypertensive tachycardic emergency requires titratable IV treatment and invasive monitoring.

IV nicardipine, then add esmolol after pressure normalizes: Nicardipine is useful after rate control; vasodilation first can provoke reflex tachycardia and increase aortic impulse.

IV nitroprusside followed by oral metoprolol: Nitroprusside is an adjunct after adequate rate control; oral beta-blockade does not provide the initial rapid titration needed here.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: A patient with acute type B dissection has active severe bronchospasm, HR 118/min and preserved LV systolic function, without shock or AV block. Which IV agent is the most appropriate alternative for initial rate control?
options: Nicardipine
Diltiazem
Nitroprusside
Amiodarone
questions.explanation:
Rate Control When Beta-Blockade Is Unsuitable

Correct answer: Diltiazem

Alternative Strategy

**IV non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockade** can substitute when beta-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated.

Diltiazem or verapamil slows AV nodal conduction and reduces rate; titrate under continuous monitoring.

Patient Selection

**Preserved ventricular function and adequate pressure matter.**

Avoid this strategy in decompensated systolic failure, significant AV block or hypotension.

**Reassess pressure after rate control.**

Add a titratable vasodilator if needed; maintain organ perfusion and coordinate definitive aortic management.

**This acute alternative does not imply chronic preference** for calcium-channel blockers in every inherited aortopathy.

Nicardipine: Nicardipine lowers pressure but does not reliably suppress heart rate; it is added once impulse control is established.

Nitroprusside: Nitroprusside rapidly reduces afterload but may trigger reflex tachycardia; it does not replace initial rate control.

Amiodarone: Amiodarone treats selected tachyarrhythmias; this sinus tachycardia needs impulse control rather than antiarrhythmic conversion.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: A patient has confirmed acute type A aortic dissection, hemopericardium and tamponade. An emergency aortic surgical team is ready. Which definitive strategy is most appropriate?
options: Completely evacuate the hemopericardium percutaneously before aortic repair
Create a pericardial window, followed by staged aortic repair
Perform controlled small-volume pericardiocentesis before proceeding to aortic repair
Emergency aortic repair with operative management of the tamponade
questions.explanation:
Aortic Dissection With Hemopericardium

Correct answer: Emergency aortic repair with operative management of the tamponade

Recognize a Surgical Cause of Tamponade

questions.question: Despite analgesia and controlled HR/BP, a patient with acute type B dissection develops rising lactate, abdominal pain and reduced superior mesenteric artery perfusion. The anatomy is suitable for endovascular treatment. What is the best next strategy?
options: Continue anti-impulse therapy with repeat imaging in one week
Urgent TEVAR-based repair with assessment of residual branch malperfusion
Isolated superior mesenteric thrombolysis without aortic treatment
Routine open descending replacement as the preferred first procedure
questions.explanation:
Complicated Type B Aortic Dissection

Correct answer: Urgent TEVAR-based repair with assessment of residual branch malperfusion

Recognize Complication

**Malperfusion, rupture, extension, progressive enlargement, refractory pain or uncontrolled BP** require escalation.

Normal arm pressure does not establish visceral perfusion; monitor lactate and organ function.

Restore Flow

**TEVAR covers the proximal tear** and expands the true lumen when anatomy permits.

**Check branch vessels after aortic treatment.**

Static obstruction may persist and need fenestration or branch intervention; bowel viability may require surgical assessment.

**Continue anti-impulse therapy and surveillance.**

Intervention does not remove every residual dissected segment or future aneurysm risk.

Continue anti-impulse therapy with repeat imaging in one week: Medical management is initial treatment for uncomplicated disease; evolving mesenteric ischemia demands urgent intervention rather than scheduled surveillance.

Isolated superior mesenteric thrombolysis without aortic treatment: Thrombolysis treats selected thrombotic occlusions; flap-related malperfusion requires correcting aortic/branch anatomy and carries bleeding concerns.

Routine open descending replacement as the preferred first procedure: Open repair remains important when endovascular treatment is unsuitable or fails; suitable complicated type B anatomy generally favors TEVAR.

questions.question: A stable patient with acute type B dissection has no pain, rupture or organ malperfusion after treatment. CTA shows total aortic diameter 43 mm and false-lumen diameter 24 mm. Which statement best reflects the 2022 ACC/AHA approach?
options: These are high-risk imaging features; selected pre-emptive endovascular management may be considered
These measurements establish rupture and mandate immediate open repair
These measurements prove branch malperfusion and require branch stenting
These measurements have no role until chronic diameter reaches 55 mm
questions.explanation:
High-Risk Uncomplicated Type B Dissection

Correct answer: These are high-risk imaging features; selected pre-emptive endovascular management may be considered

Risk Features

**Examples:** maximal aorta ==>40 mm==; false lumen ==>20–22 mm==; entry tear ==>10 mm==.

Other findings include lesser-curvature entry, interval enlargement, bloody effusion or imaging-only malperfusion.

Qualified Intervention

**Initially uncomplicated does not mean low long-term risk.**

Selected TEVAR can be considered after expert assessment; it is not mandatory for every uncomplicated case.

**Balance remodeling benefit against procedural risk.**

Consider landing zones, connective-tissue disease, stroke/spinal injury risk and follow-up capacity; continue medical treatment whichever pathway is chosen.

These measurements establish rupture and mandate immediate open repair: Rupture requires hemorrhage or other rupture evidence; enlargement markers alone identify risk, not established rupture.

These measurements prove branch malperfusion and require branch stenting: Branch malperfusion depends on vascular and organ findings; the patient has no supplied perfusion deficit.

These measurements have no role until chronic diameter reaches 55 mm: High-risk acute morphology can inform earlier multidisciplinary decisions; chronic aneurysm thresholds do not exhaust the acute assessment.

questions.question: Noncontrast CT shows crescentic hyperattenuating thickening of the ascending aortic wall. Contrast imaging shows no opacified false lumen or visible intimal flap. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Type A intramural hematoma
Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer
Aortic pseudoaneurysm
Uncomplicated mural thrombus
questions.explanation:
Aortic Intramural Hematoma

Correct answer: Type A intramural hematoma

Imaging Pattern

**Intramural blood without a perfused false lumen** can produce acute aortic syndrome.

Absence of a visible flap does not make the lesion benign; progression to dissection or rupture can occur.

Management by Location

**Ascending involvement generally prompts urgent surgical management.**

Selected high-operative-risk type A cases without high-risk imaging may be managed expectantly in expert centers, not by routine outpatient observation.

**Uncomplicated type B IMH can start with medical treatment.**

Complications or high-risk progression change the intervention threshold; noncontrast and contrast CT provide complementary information.

Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer: An ulcer is a focal contrast-filled crater penetrating atherosclerotic intima; the supplied lesion is crescentic mural blood without that crater.

Aortic pseudoaneurysm: Pseudoaneurysm is a contained wall disruption with an outpouching communicating with the lumen; no focal outpouching is described.

Uncomplicated mural thrombus: Luminal thrombus lies within the intimal boundary and usually lacks the characteristic acute hyperattenuating intramural crescent.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: After successful proximal repair of type A dissection, a patient has a residual dissected descending aorta. Which CT/MRI schedule is recommended by the 2022 ACC/AHA guideline if findings remain stable?
options: At 12 months, then only for recurrent symptoms
At 6 months, then every three years
At 1, 6 and 12 months, then annually
Every month for the first year, then every five years
questions.explanation:
Surveillance After Aortic Dissection

Correct answer: At 1, 6 and 12 months, then annually

Why Follow-up Continues

**Repair treats the immediate segment, not the entire aortopathy.**

Residual false-lumen flow, distal expansion and new aneurysm formation may require later intervention.

Long-Term Care

**CT or MRI at 1, 6, 12 months and annually if stable.**

New symptoms or growth require earlier evaluation; compare consistent measurement planes and techniques.

**Continue BP/heart-rate control**, commonly beta-blockade with additional agents as needed.

**Assess familial disease and counsel activity.**

Screen relatives when appropriate; avoid intense isometric strain and individualize aerobic activity and pregnancy planning.

At 12 months, then only for recurrent symptoms: Aortic enlargement may be asymptomatic; symptom-driven imaging misses progressive residual disease after proximal repair.

At 6 months, then every three years: Long intervals may suit selected small stable aneurysms; residual dissection requires earlier and continuing annual cross-sectional assessment.

Every month for the first year, then every five years: Monthly imaging is not the standard stable follow-up schedule, and five-year intervals are too long for residual dissection.

questions.question: A 42-year-old has a root aneurysm and a father who died from aortic dissection. A multigene panel finds no pathogenic variant. What should be offered to first-degree relatives?
options: Aortic imaging despite the negative genetic panel
Imaging only if a relative develops hypertension
Cascade testing of a variant of uncertain significance as a definitive risk classifier
No screening because the genetic panel excludes inherited disease
questions.explanation:
Family Screening in Thoracic Aortic Disease

Correct answer: Aortic imaging despite the negative genetic panel

Genetic Evaluation

**Young presentation, syndromic features or family history** support genetic counseling and testing.

A pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant enables targeted cascade testing; a VUS requires cautious interpretation.

Imaging Relatives

**Screen first-degree relatives with TTE**, adding CT/MRI when the root or ascending aorta is incompletely seen.

**Negative genetic testing does not exclude heritability.**

Determine repeat imaging from age, baseline dimensions and family events.

**Recognize gene–phenotype patterns:** FBN1 in Marfan; TGFBR1/2 in Loeys–Dietz; COL3A1 in vascular Ehlers–Danlos; ACTA2 in nonsyndromic familial disease.

Imaging only if a relative develops hypertension: Hypertension raises risk but is not required for familial thoracic aortopathy; waiting for it can miss silent dilation.

Cascade testing of a variant of uncertain significance as a definitive risk classifier: A VUS does not establish a disease-causing genotype and should not replace phenotype-based family imaging.

No screening because the genetic panel excludes inherited disease: Current panels do not identify every causal variant; a negative result cannot negate the strongly suggestive family history.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106

questions.question: A 67-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history, now abstinent, has no abdominal symptoms and no prior aortic imaging. What screening test is appropriate?
options: Contrast abdominal CT as the initial screening test
One-time abdominal aortic ultrasound
Abdominal MRI every year beginning now
No screening after smoking cessation
questions.explanation:
Screening for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm

Correct answer: One-time abdominal aortic ultrasound

Eligibility

**Men aged ≥65 who have ever smoked** are a standard ACC/AHA screening group.

Family history also informs screening; other organizations specify different age windows and selective eligibility.

Interpret and Act

**AAA is conventionally diameter ==≥3.0 cm==.**

Document maximal diameter with a consistent measurement convention; body size and morphology can modify clinical interpretation.

**Ultrasound is first-line for screening and surveillance.**

Use CT when ultrasound is inadequate or detailed anatomy is needed.

**Screening is preventive, not an emergency pathway.**

Pain, shock or suspected rupture requires immediate clinical/vascular assessment rather than routine screening scheduling.

Contrast abdominal CT as the initial screening test: CTA is valuable for symptomatic disease and repair planning; ultrasound provides screening without contrast or radiation.

Abdominal MRI every year beginning now: MRI can characterize aortic disease but is unnecessary as repeated screening in an otherwise eligible unscreened asymptomatic patient.

No screening after smoking cessation: Ever-smoking remains an eligibility factor; cessation improves risk but does not erase the accumulated aneurysm risk.

questions.question: An asymptomatic woman has a stable fusiform infrarenal AAA measuring 4.6 cm, with no rapid growth. Under the 2022 ACC/AHA framework, what is the usual ultrasound surveillance interval?
options: Every 12 months
Every 3 years
Every 6 months
Every 24 months
questions.explanation:
Sex-Specific AAA Surveillance

Correct answer: Every 6 months

Surveillance

**Sex-specific intervals reflect different rupture risks at a given diameter.**

This ==4.6 cm== aneurysm falls in the six-month group, not the male ==4.0–4.9 cm== annual group.

Change the Plan When Needed

**New attributable pain or rapid enlargement** triggers earlier evaluation, regardless of the scheduled interval.

**Use reproducible measurements.**

Small differences between modalities or planes may reflect technique; confirm clinically important growth.

**Treat vascular risk:** smoking cessation, BP control and atherosclerotic risk reduction; these do not replace surveillance.

Diameter | Interval

3.0–3.9 cm, either sex | 3 years

Men 4.0–4.9; women 4.0–4.4 cm | 1 year

Men ≥5.0; women ≥4.5 cm | 6 months

Every 12 months: Annual imaging applies to women with 4.0–4.4 cm AAA; women at 4.5 cm or greater need shorter surveillance.

Every 3 years: Three-year surveillance applies to uncomplicated 3.0–3.9 cm AAA; this lesion is substantially closer to the female repair threshold.

Every 24 months: Two-year intervals are not the recommended schedule for a woman with a 4.6 cm AAA approaching intervention size.

questions.question: A low-risk patient is scheduled for surgery for symptomatic severe aortic regurgitation. Cross-sectional imaging confirms a maximal ascending aortic diameter of 48 mm. Under ESC 2025 guidance, what should the surgical plan include?
options: Isolated valve surgery with aortic intervention deferred until fifty-five millimeters
Assessment for concomitant replacement of the enlarged ascending aorta
Isolated valve surgery with aortic replacement considered only if subsequent rapid growth occurs
Plan a root replacement instead of evaluating the tubular ascending segment
questions.explanation:
Addressing Aortic Disease During Valve Surgery

Correct answer: Assessment for concomitant replacement of the enlarged ascending aorta

Concomitant Aortic Assessment

**Valve disease and aortic disease require a combined anatomical plan.** The root and tubular ascending segment are different structures and should be measured and described separately.

ESC 2025 advises considering concomitant root or ascending replacement at maximal diameter ≥45 mm when a valve operation is indicated and predicted surgical risk is low.

This is not a universal isolated-aorta threshold. Etiology, genetic disease, growth, body size, family history and operative circumstances influence aortic decisions.

Repair, Replacement and Valve Preservation

**Choose the operation according to the mechanism and the involved aortic segment.** Root enlargement with suitable pliable cusps may allow valve-sparing root replacement at an experienced center.

Calcification, cusp destruction or an unlikely durable repair may favor valve replacement. A tubular ascending graft and an operation on the root are not interchangeable labels.

Review CT or CMR alongside echocardiographic valve assessment and discuss durability, prosthesis implications and reintervention. A successful isolated correction of regurgitation does not remove untreated aortic risk. Conversely, a forty-eight-millimeter ascending measurement does not by itself prove that every part of the root must be replaced. The clinical value of the threshold is to prompt an integrated surgical decision rather than two disconnected treatment plans.

Isolated valve surgery with aortic intervention deferred until fifty-five millimeters: An isolated aortopathy threshold should not be copied into a patient already undergoing valve surgery; concomitant replacement can be considered at a lower diameter with low predicted surgical risk.

Isolated valve surgery with aortic replacement considered only if subsequent rapid growth occurs: Rapid growth is an important aortopathy risk feature, but the opportunity for concomitant replacement at the specified size should be assessed during the already indicated operation rather than reserved solely for documented future growth.

Plan a root replacement instead of evaluating the tubular ascending segment: Root replacement is relevant to root pathology; a tubular ascending measurement does not establish root enlargement. The operation should address the demonstrated segment and valve mechanism.

Thresholds

**Marfan root replacement:** recommended at ==≥5.0 cm==; reasonable at ==≥4.5 cm== with high-risk features.

Family dissection, rapid growth and adverse root/aortic morphology inform individualized decisions.

**Infective aortitis/aneurysm:** bacteremia plus compatible wall or periaortic changes.

Salmonella and S. aureus are important causes; obtain cultures and assess other infectious foci.

**Antibiotics and aortic source control are coordinated.**

Prolonged IV therapy is generally at least six weeks, individualized by organism, repair and persistent infection.

**Repair timing and technique depend on instability and anatomy.**

Open debridement/reconstruction or selected endovascular bridging/treatment needs expert discussion; infection surveillance remains essential.

**“Mycotic” does not mean fungal**; most such aneurysms are bacterial.

High-dose glucocorticoids for presumed sterile inflammatory aneurysm: Sterile periaortitis can require immunosuppression; bacteremia and an evolving saccular lesion favor infection, which steroids could worsen.

Elective repair only after the usual fusiform diameter threshold is reached: Degenerative size thresholds do not safely govern infected aneurysms; infection can cause rapid wall destruction and rupture at smaller sizes.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man has new persistent abdominal and back pain, a tender 4.8 cm infrarenal AAA and no alternative cause on CTA. There is no free rupture and he is stable. What is the best next step?
options: Admit for urgent vascular repair assessment and monitored optimization
Continue six-month ultrasound surveillance because diameter is below 5.5 cm
Treat pain and reassess after a routine outpatient interval
Begin therapeutic anticoagulation for mural thrombus as the principal treatment
questions.explanation:
Symptomatic AAA Below the Elective Size Threshold

Correct answer: Admit for urgent vascular repair assessment and monitored optimization

Symptomatic Disease

**Attributable pain or tenderness warrants repair evaluation irrespective of usual elective diameter.**

Exclude alternative diagnoses, contained rupture and infection; absence of free rupture does not establish benign disease.

Immediate Care

**Monitor, control pain and BP, and involve the vascular team.**

Stable patients permit rapid anatomical planning and optimization; deterioration requires emergency intervention.

**CTA defines anatomy and complications.**

Aneurysm-related embolization, fistulation or rapid growth can also justify intervention below standard fusiform thresholds.

**Long-term care continues after repair:** tobacco cessation, cardiovascular prevention and procedure-specific surveillance.

Continue six-month ultrasound surveillance because diameter is below 5.5 cm: Size-based surveillance applies to asymptomatic stable aneurysms; new attributable pain changes the repair indication.

Treat pain and reassess after a routine outpatient interval: Analgesia is supportive but does not remove the risk signaled by a newly symptomatic aneurysm; inpatient urgent evaluation is needed.

Begin therapeutic anticoagulation for mural thrombus as the principal treatment: Mural thrombus is common within AAA; it is not by itself an indication for anticoagulation or an explanation permitting delayed repair assessment.

ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106
